Affiliation:: Department of Mathematics, University of Oklahoma
Data & Platforms: Stepper motor driven torsion spring setup
Application Areas: Predictive monitoring of slip events and intermittent dynamics in granular materials
Quantitative reconstruction of internal stress and force networks in photoelastic media
Data-driven characterization of global dynamics and invariant sets in nonlinear systems
Industrial process control in agriculture, construction, and chemical industries via granular flow analysis
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Transfer Learning for Physics-Informed Inverse Problems: Leveraging pre-trained deep learning architectures on synthetic data to solve computationally expensive inverse problems in physical systems, specifically using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to reconstruct inter-particle forces from photoelastic images with ~10% mean absolute percentage error, bypassing traditional optimization bottlenecks.

Topological Data Analysis for Dynamic Precursor Detection: Applying persistent homology and Wasserstein distance metrics to force network graphs to identify non-linear, mesoscale fluctuations that serve as precursors to macroscopic slip events, revealing that local topological generators increase consistently before failure while global averages remain insensitive.

Machine-Learned Phase Space Discretization: Utilizing neural networks to learn compact cubical decompositions of phase space from labeled orbit data, enabling the robust computation of Conley indices and identification of attracting neighborhoods with significantly reduced computational complexity compared to regular grid methods.

Multi-Scale Force Network Characterization: Integrating experimental photoelasticity (G2 method) with discrete element simulations to construct differential force networks, analyzing their evolution during stick-slip dynamics to distinguish between static restructuring and dynamic yielding in quasi-static deformations.
Summary Description: Miroslav Kramar is a computational physicist and mathematician specializing in the intersection of granular media physics, topological data analysis, and machine learning. His research focuses on characterizing intermittent dynamics, such as stick-slip motion and force chain evolution, in granular materials. He employs photoelasticity and discrete element simulations to generate data, which he analyzes using persistent homology to detect precursors to slip events. Additionally, he develops machine learning frameworks, including CNNs for force reconstruction and neural network-based phase space discretization, to robustly identify invariant sets and global dynamics in nonlinear systems. His work bridges experimental mechanics and computational topology, offering new tools for predicting failure in soft matter and industrial granular processes.
